verses.translation_literal: A psalm of David. YHWH, I have called you; hasten to me; give ear [to] my voice when I call to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of David, offered at the edge of fear. LORD, I am calling you. Come quickly. Come to me now. Bend your ear to my voice, to this cry I am sending up to you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with three short commands in a row: hasten, give ear, and the plea is made while the speaker is still calling. Play it breathless, not polite. The Hebrew says it is urgent: חוּשָׁה, 'make haste', is the word of the emergency prayer in Psalm 22:20 and 38:23 (the packet's Metzudat Zion links it to Psalm 22). It is also not a quiet devotion; the speaker presses God to listen while the voice is still in the air. Malbim catches this: 'give ear' at the start of my calling, not after the end of it.

The KJV 'make haste unto me' is faithful, but its 'I cry unto thee' is a softer verb than the Hebrew; קָרָא is simply 'to call', to summon someone as one would call a neighbor to a fire. 'Psalm of David' (מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד) names the genre: a מִזְמוֹר is a song sung with strings, from the root זמר. Note that the English Bibles count this heading as verse 0 and start the prayer at 141:1; the Hebrew counts it as part of verse 1.

philological_notes.note: 'Hasten!', a command to God to act at once; the same imperative begins the urgent prayers of Psalms 22:20 and 38:23. It makes God the one who has to hurry, where the speaker has no time.
'Give ear': a verb made from the noun אֹזֶן, 'ear', so literally 'ear it', 'make your ear [attend]'. English 'give ear' keeps the body-word that the verb is built from.

verses.translation_literal: May my prayer be established [as] incense before you, the lifting of my palms [as] an evening offering.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let my prayer stand before you like rising incense, steady and fragrant. Let my hands, lifted open in the dusk, be received as the evening offering.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the speaker turns the body into a temple. Prayer becomes incense, and the raised palms become the evening מִנְחָה, the offering that closed the day's service at the altar. Neither noun has the word 'like' in the Hebrew; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri all say the particle כ is understood. Keep it blunt on stage: my prayer, incense; my hands, offering. The metaphor is a claim.

The KJV 'be set forth' blurs תִּכּוֹן, from כּוּן, 'to be firm, fixed, prepared'. The prayer is to be set in place, made ready and standing, as the incense was laid on the altar (BBE 'ordered' is closer). KJV renders מִנְחָה 'sacrifice', and that has support: מִנְחָה is literally a 'gift' (Metzudat Zion), and in the priestly laws it is a grain offering, but Meiri and Metzudat David both take the evening one as the daily tamid, the lamb offered between the afternoons, so a reader hearing 'sacrifice' is not misled. What English loses is the plain word 'gift': the hands are held out empty, as a present. Radak adds that the psalm may have been composed in the evening; Malbim notes that the evening offering came last, after all the other services. The lifting of palms is the standard posture of Israelite prayer (Ps 28:2, 63:5).

philological_notes.note: Incense, the fragrant smoke burned on the inner altar morning and evening; the prayer rises like it. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri supply an understood 'like' (כקטרת).

A מִנְחָה is a gift, literally (Metzudat Zion); in the priestly laws it is typically a grain offering. Metzudat David identifies the evening מִנְחָה with the daily tamid offering and Meiri likewise calls it the tamid, so KJV 'sacrifice' has traditional support. Meiri also offers a second reading, from the root of 'sweet': a heart laid out like a pleasing gift (Mal 3:4).

verses.translation_literal: Set, YHWH, a guard for my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips.
verses.translation_dramatic: Set a guard on my mouth, LORD. Stand a sentry at the door of my lips, and let nothing pass them that you have not let pass.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker asks to be policed. A mouth is a city gate; lips are its door, and a watchman is posted so that nothing leaves unchecked. The Hebrew uses two different words for the guard, שָׁמְרָה and נִצְּרָה, and the tradition divides on why. Radak and Metzudat David say the verse simply doubles the request in different words, Metzudat David adding that the doubling shows how great the need for guarding is. Meiri hears two requests: the first for the speech itself to be set right and kept from error, the second, 'over the door of my lips', for the words once they are at the lips, since a true thought can still slip out wrongly as it leaves. Malbim reads a step up: the first is a keeper at the mouth, the second a watcher who stops even the lifting of the lips, since נוֹצֵר is stronger than שׁוֹמֵר. Radak also notes that lips are called a door because they open and close.

The KJV 'set a watch ... before my mouth' is good English, but 'watch' in 1611 meant a watchman or guard; modern readers hear a clock or an hour. The word דַּל for 'door' is rare (the usual word is דֶּלֶת); Ibn Ezra and Radak gloss it as 'door', Rashi as the upper lip, and Metzudat Zion links it to the root of 'lifted', as in Isaiah 38:14. Either way, the image is architecture: a speaker who knows that words, once out of the gate, cannot be called back.

philological_notes.note: A rare form, found only here. Radak takes it as a noun, 'a guard', built like חָכְמָה; Meiri records the noun reading but finds it distant and prefers an understood verb ('set your heart on me and guard my mouth'); Ibn Ezra reads an elided object, as in 'set a muzzle'. I keep a noun.

'The door of my lips'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read דַּל as a short form of דֶּלֶת, 'door', for the lips that open and shut; Rashi takes it as the upper lip; Metzudat Zion prefers 'lifting'. The common word דַּל means 'poor', which a hearer may catch as an undertone; that is my own hearing, not a source's.

verses.translation_literal: Do not turn my heart to an evil thing, to practice practices in wickedness with men, workers of iniquity; and let me not eat in their delicacies.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not bend my heart toward anything evil, toward deeds of wickedness done in company with men who make a trade of crime. And let me never sit at their table, never taste their delicacies.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the mouth to the heart: the second request is about desire. In Hebrew thought the heart is the seat of will and mind, and the speaker asks God not to tilt it, as one tilts a scale or a branch. The danger is not an act but a drift toward company: 'with men', who are workers of אָוֶן, trouble and iniquity. The last line moves to the table. To eat their delicacies is to be their guest and their accomplice; in the ancient Near East, sharing a meal sealed an alliance. Radak and Metzudat David say the delicacies stand for the pull of worldly pleasure.

The KJV 'practise wicked works' misses the sound play of לְהִתְעוֹלֵל עֲלִלוֹת: 'to do deeds' with a doubled root, an intensive form that suggests habitual, deliberate doing (YLT: 'do habitually'). The English 'practice practices' keeps the doubling. KJV's 'dainties' is archaic for מַנְעַמִּים, from the root of 'pleasant'; and 'let me not eat' is correct for אֶלְחַם from לחם, 'to eat', not 'to fight'.

philological_notes.note: A figura etymologica: the verb and its object share the root, 'to do deeds'. The reflexive-intensive stem makes it a deliberate, repeated doing; Metzudat Zion compares 'what was done to me' in Lamentations 1:22.
'I will eat': the root meaning 'bread, food', not the homonym 'to fight'. Ibn Ezra glosses it as eating and Metzudat Zion says every food is called 'bread'.

'Their delicacies, their pleasantnesses', from the root of 'pleasant'. It is a plural of the root that is also used for the 'sweet' words of verse 6, so the reader can hear a link between the wicked's delights and the speaker's words.

verses.translation_literal: Let a righteous [man] strike me, [in] loyalty, and let him rebuke me: oil of the head, let my head not refuse it; for still, and my prayer [is] against their evil deeds.
verses.translation_dramatic: If a righteous man strikes me, let it be a kindness; if he rebukes me, let it be oil poured on my head, and let my head not turn it away. But their wicked deeds I will meet with prayer, and I am praying still.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hardest verse of the psalm, and the actor should know it is a crux and not hide the roughness. The speaker would rather be struck by a good man than feasted by bad ones. The blow is a חֶסֶד, an act of covenant loyalty; the rebuke is 'head oil', the fine oil poured over a guest's head at a banquet (Ps 23:5), the opposite of the wicked's table in verse 4. Rashi sees the oil as the oil of royal anointing; Ibn Ezra reads it instead as the wicked's own perfumed oil; Malbim ties it to David's pang of conscience at cutting Saul's cloak.

The KJV keeps the wish ('Let the righteous smite me') but then supplies 'it shall be' before 'a kindness' and again before 'an excellent oil', turning two wishes into assurances, and ends 'which shall not break my head'. That last sense, a head broken by the blow, follows Radak and Ibn Ezra, who take the head not to be broken. The Hebrew verb יָנִי is from נוא, 'to refuse, hold back' (compare Numbers 30:6, cited by Metzudat Zion), and that is the sense followed here: let my head not refuse the oil. The final clause כִּי־עוֹד וּתְפִלָּתִי בְּרָעוֹתֵיהֶם is unclear; the most natural reading is 'my prayer is still against their evil deeds'.

philological_notes.note: 'Let him strike me': a heavy, hammering blow, as in Judges 5:26 where Metzudat Zion compares it with Jael's blow against Sisera. A jussive, a wish. KJV keeps 'Let ... smite me' but adds 'it shall be' before the next phrase, which makes a promise of what is a wish.

'May it refuse': from נוא, 'to refuse, frustrate, withhold', as in Numbers 30:6 (so Metzudat Zion, whom I follow). Radak and Ibn Ezra instead read 'may it not break my head', taking the oil as the remedy for a blow; Ibn Ezra sees the verb as the opposite of 'let him strike'; Meiri reads it as written with an aleph, יניא.

'Oil of the head': either oil poured on the head, or 'choice oil' (as in רֹאשׁ בְּשָׂמִים, 'chief spices', Exodus 30:23, cited by Radak and Meiri). The Hebrew word רֹאשׁ means both 'head' and 'chief', a doubling the verse plays on.

verses.translation_literal: Their judges have been thrown down at the hands of a rock, and they will hear my words, for they are pleasant.
verses.translation_dramatic: Their judges are flung down, down into the hands of the rock. And then they will listen to what I say, and find my words sweet.
verses.directors_commentary:
A scene of sudden violence, and almost nothing in it is certain, so do not play it as though it were. The judges (שֹׁפְטֵיהֶם) are the leaders of the wicked, not necessarily magistrates in a court; they are 'thrown down' (נִשְׁמְטוּ, 'let drop, hurled'), and the phrase 'at the hands of the rock' is odd. Radak and Meiri allow a curse: may their leaders be hurled from the cliff. Rashi takes the 'rock' as the hardness of the heart, a 'stone heart'; Malbim and Metzudat David set it on the famous 'rock of division' where Saul turned back from David.

The KJV 'in stony places' is a guess that turns the rock into a landscape, and 'are overthrown' a past event. The Hebrew says 'hands', the same word used for 'power': the judges fall into the power of the rock, or of the Rock (God). The second half is gentler: when the leaders are gone, the people will hear, and the speaker's words are נָעֵמוּ, 'pleasant', the root of the 'delicacies' they would not eat in verse 4. The contrast of sweet words and hard rock is the point.

philological_notes.note: 'They were hurled down' or 'released, let fall'. The root means to drop or let go (2 Samuel 6:6, of oxen that stumbled, as Metzudat Zion notes). Radak and Meiri read the perfect as a curse about the future.

Literally 'in the hands of a rock': by the sides of the cliff (ASV), into the power of the rock, or the hardness of heart (Rashi, from Ezekiel 11:19). Malbim and Metzudat David identify the rock with the 'rock of division' (1 Samuel 23:28).

verses.translation_literal: Like one who plows and breaks up in the earth, our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol.
verses.translation_dramatic: As when the plowman cuts the soil and the clods fly apart, so our bones lie scattered at the mouth of Sheol.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood falls from judgment to ruin, and the speaker says 'our', not 'my'. The image is of the earth split open: bones strewn like clods or splinters, and the mouth of Sheol, the underworld, is the gaping crack. The scattered bones here are an ugly picture, because an Israelite was supposed to be gathered to his ancestors, in a tomb, with bones in place; to lie unburied and strewn about was the worst end. Radak reads it as hyperbole about fear and trembling, bones coming apart (compare Psalm 22:15).

The KJV adds 'wood': 'as when one cutteth and cleaveth wood upon the earth', which turns a plowman into a woodcutter. Rashi and Radak do supply 'wood', but the Hebrew has only the two verbs and 'in the earth', and the verbs פָּלַח and בָּקַע can both be used of cutting or ploughing the ground. Sheol is not 'the grave' (KJV) in a modern sense; it is the realm of the dead, with its own mouth, a place that swallows. YLT's 'at the command of Saul' mistakes שְׁאוֹל for שָׁאוּל, which is only a vowel apart in unpointed text.

philological_notes.note: 'One who cleaves and one who splits': two near-synonyms (Metzudat Zion, Radak). The object may be wood (so Rashi) or the soil; פלח is used of splitting the kidneys in Job 16:13 (cited by Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion).

'At the mouth of Sheol', the opening of the underworld. פֶּה means 'mouth' and 'edge'; Sheol is pictured as a gaping throat. Not 'at the command of Saul' (YLT): that reads the name שָׁאוּל for שְׁאוֹל.

verses.translation_literal: For to you, YHWH, my Lord, [are] my eyes; in you I have taken refuge; do not pour out my life.
verses.translation_dramatic: But my eyes are on you, LORD, my Lord. In you I have taken shelter. Do not let my life be poured out.
verses.directors_commentary:
The turn. After the bones and the rock the eyes lift to God, and the title is doubled: YHWH, Adonai, 'LORD, my Lord'. The speaker has stopped looking at the wicked and looks up, the posture of a servant waiting for a sign (Psalm 123:2). Rashi ties this verse back to the two requests about the mouth and the heart: because my eyes are on you, guard me. 'Take refuge' (חָסָה) is the verb of the bird or the fugitive under a wing or a rock, the opposite of the trap and net coming in the next verses.

The KJV 'leave not my soul destitute' renders אַל־תְּעַר נַפְשִׁי, from עָרָה, 'to pour out, to empty, to lay bare'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion all cite Rebekah emptying her jar into the trough (Genesis 24:20), so the picture is of the life poured out like water, spilled and gone. Metzudat David calls it a figure: when the life leaves the body it is as though it were poured out; Meiri compares Hannah's 'I poured out my soul' (1 Samuel 1:15). 'Soul' is נֶפֶשׁ, 'life, throat, self', not an immortal soul. The KJV 'God the Lord' for the double divine name follows an old convention of rendering יהוה אדני as 'the Lord GOD'.

philological_notes.note: 'Pour out, empty': used of Rebekah emptying her jar (Genesis 24:20), cited by Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion. Rashi glosses 'do not send my life away from before you'; Metzudat David and Radak read it as the life poured out of the body. KJV 'leave destitute' is a different reading, 'lay bare'.
'My life, my self'. What is poured out is the life itself; Meiri links it to Hannah's 'I poured out my soul before YHWH', where the same image describes prayer.

The divine name written with the vowels of אֱלֹהִים, because it stands next to אֲדֹנָי, so that the reader does not say the name twice. The consonants are the divine name; the pointing is a reading instruction.

verses.translation_literal: Keep me from the hands of the trap [that] they have laid for me, and the snares of workers of iniquity.
verses.translation_dramatic: Keep me out of the trap's grip, the one they have laid for me, and out of the snares of those who work iniquity.
verses.directors_commentary:
The hunter's vocabulary begins. A פַּח is a bird-trap, a spring net on the ground; a מוֹקֵשׁ is the bait-stick or trigger that sets it off, so 'snares' and 'trap' are two parts of one device. Hear the repeated sounds of יָקְשׁוּ (they set the trap) and מוֹקְשׁוֹת (snares), from the same root: the trap and the verb of laying it. The workers of אָוֶן come back from verse 4, closing a loop: the men whose delicacies he refused are the men who lay the traps.

The KJV 'gins' is an archaism for snares (a gin is an engine, a trap); readers today do not know it. The Hebrew says 'from the hands of the trap', as though the trap had hands that grab. Malbim reads מוֹקֵשׁ as the trigger inside the net, and Radak suggests the second clause may be the same thing repeated.

philological_notes.note: A bird-trap or net on the ground; the figure of a hidden danger. 'Hands of the trap' personifies the device.

'They set' and 'snares' share the root יקש, 'to lay a trap': a verb and its noun in one line. The noun is plural (מוֹקְשׁוֹת), a rare form. Metzudat David reads the plural as many kinds of schemes, Radak as a doubling.

verses.translation_literal: Let wicked [men] fall into his nets together, I, until I pass by.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the wicked fall, all of them together, into his nets, and let me go on past, until I am through.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a reversal of the hunt: the hunters are caught in the very net, and the speaker walks past it. The Hebrew picture is quiet and almost comic: the nets close on the wicked 'together' (יַחַד) while 'I' (אָנֹכִי, the long, emphatic form of the pronoun) simply go by. There is no battle, only a man who is not where the trap expects him. Radak notes that the singular 'his nets' points at one leader, Saul, with the plural 'wicked' his followers; Meiri names Saul or Doeg.

The KJV 'their own nets' smooths the singular, and its 'whilst that I withal escape' is a paraphrase in old speech: 'withal' means 'at the same time'. The Hebrew has עַד־אֶעֱבוֹר, 'until I pass over', and does not say 'escape'. The verb עָבַר, 'to cross over', is the word for crossing a river or a boundary. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David reorder the phrase as 'until I pass', meaning that they fall into the net before I reach it, so that when I pass it is no longer spread; Malbim reads a gentler wish, that they be held in the net, not killed, until David and his men get away.

philological_notes.note: 'His nets': a fisher's or hunter's net (Habakkuk 1:15 uses the singular מִכְמֶרֶת, cited by Metzudat Zion). The suffix is singular 'his' after plural 'wicked'; Radak takes it as Saul, the leader; Meiri as the chief enemy.

'Until I pass by or over'. עבר is to cross a boundary or a river; the verse gives no object, so 'escape' (KJV) is an interpretation. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David reorder it as 'until I pass', meaning before I pass the trap.
